name: Square du Vert-Galant
short_description: Triangular pocket-park at the western tip of Ile de la Cite, sitting roughly seven meters below modern street level and pointing downstream beneath the Pont Neuf.

beats.script_body:
The leafy green triangular square behind the Pont Neuf is named for Henri IV, the lusty gallant on horseback who loved his city mightily, especially its wine, women, and good times. This romantic western tip of the boat-shaped Île de la Cité is the original settlement of the Parisii, a Celtic tribe subdued by Caesar — the Romans called it Lutetia, or Cara Lutetia, "my beloved Lutetia," in the words of the late Roman emperor Julian in 358 AD.

As king, le Vert Galant (1589–1610) declared his intention "to make this city beautiful, tranquil, desiring to make a whole world of this city and a wonder of the world." Such triumphs as the elegant Pont Neuf — the "new bridge" is the oldest bridge in Paris — the Place Dauphine opposite the bridge, and the Place Royale (later renamed Place des Vosges) show his genius as architect and urban visionary. His energetic love life — he had two wives, at least fifty-six mistresses, and households full of bastards — also won him the heart of Parisians, until his serial amours began to bore and irritate.

But Henri the obsessive lover was above all a peacemaker. Born and raised a Protestant by a rigidly reformist mother, he converted to Catholicism, the religion of the majority, to end the long religious wars between Catholics and Protestants that by the end of the sixteenth century had left Paris starving and looking like a bomb site. Detesting religious partisanship, he drafted and signed the Edict of Nantes (1598), which put toleration of the religion he had renounced on the books. The fanatical Catholic who stabbed him to death, Francis Ravaillac, was not persuaded. But to this day, together with Charlemagne, Joan of Arc, and Saint-Louis IX, Henri IV remains one of France's heroes. He declared kindness and mercy the primary virtues of a prince.

beats.script_body: Once you descend the staircase and enter the square, Vert Galant presents a magical combination of delights: a strong, wide river, flowers and grass, a riverbank shaded with willows and a prospect of magnificent architecture — the Louvre on the right and the gold-domed Institut de France on the left. There's also, in early evening in all seasons, a fair portion of privacy, a promise of intimacy.

queue_basis: An open public pocket-park with a free open gate at the island's tip; visitors walk straight down the steps with no door, ticket, or screening.

name: Place Dauphine
short_description: Triangular square created by Henri IV in 1607 on the Île de la Cité, one of Paris's most romantic hidden gems

beats.script_body: Enter through rue Henri Robert on the east side of Pont Neuf. Henri IV designed this hideaway for his son Louis XIII — the dauphin — who was nine years old when his father was assassinated. Some of the low brick buildings are of Henri's period; the trees are new and small, having only recently been planted to replace the white chestnuts that were attacked by a virulent pest. Yves Montand and Simone Signoret, who loved the village-like Place, lived here.

name: Pont des Arts
short_description: Pedestrian bridge across the Seine once famous for its love locks, connecting the Louvre to the Institut de France

beats.script_body: The footbridge connecting the Left Bank to the Louvre carries a lively traffic of musicians, painters, students, lovers, tourists, and children, with a wide view of the Seine and a rear view of the Square du Vert Galant. Pierre Auguste Renoir's painting Le Pont des Arts (1868) was the first he sold to the art dealer Paul Durand-Ruel, one of the most important advocates for French impressionists in Europe and the United States.

name: Voltaire Statue (Square Honoré-Champion)
short_description: Stone replacement statue of the philosopher Voltaire by Léon-Ernest Drivier, installed in 1962 to replace the original 1885 bronze on Quai Malaquais that was melted down by the Nazis in 1941.

beats.script_body: Through an arch to the right of the Institut de France on the Left Bank's Quai de Conti, a statue of the eighteenth-century philosopher Voltaire stands atop a small green mound bordered with flowers. Without this immensely influential leader of the Enlightenment, the Declaration of Independence (and the American Revolution) would, according to Benjamin Franklin and Thomas Jefferson, never have come to pass.

name: Square Jean XXIII
short_description: Cathedral garden on the south side of Notre-Dame, dedicated to the memory of Pope John XXIII (Angelo Roncalli), on the site of the former archbishop's palace destroyed in 1831.

beats.script_body: Until 1831, when it was destroyed in a riot, the palace of the archbishop of Paris occupied the land between Notre-Dame and the Seine. Both the palace gardens and the cathedral had long been revered sites in this quartier of religious associations dating back to the fourth century, when Emperor Julian presided in a temple dedicated to Jupiter. Those Roman ruins became the foundation of the basilica of Saint-Etienne (Saint Stephen) in 528 and the first Notre-Dame. The new Notre-Dame, begun in 1163, stands today — after centuries of renovations and the fanatical rampages of the Terror — as one of the crown jewels of Gothic architecture not only in Paris but all over Europe.

beats.script_body:
The new cathedral gardens are dedicated to the memory of Pope John XXIII, born Angelo Roncalli (1881–1963), in Lombardy — the papal nuncio in Paris from 1944 to 1953, who went on to become the "good pope" and the progenitor of the Second Vatican Council (1962–1965). "Jesus came to break down the barriers," he preached. "The central point of his teaching is love."

Parisians remember Roncalli's long walks through the city accompanied by his friends — Protestants, Catholics, Jews, agnostics, atheists. At diplomatic receptions he enjoyed the champagne and the conviviality of men and women. He read French literature and knew the post-World War II French intellectuals and theologians, whom he would invite to participate in the reforms of Vatican II. A savvy diplomat, he was trusted by the French government. On the occasion of being awarded the Legion of Honor, President Auriol praised him for understanding and respecting "the traditions of justice and tolerance," the honor of the French nation.

The inviting square beneath the flying buttresses is a fitting memorial to the genial man who confessed a deep sadness when he was recalled from Paris to Rome: "I love France and I love Paris," he told a friend, "and I hoped to stay a little longer. I can't really see myself in Rome."

beats.script_body: Flowering cherry trees, in luxuriant bloom along the south porches in April, screen but do not hide the original medallions that bear images of student life. Beds of daffodils and tulips run the length of the cathedral's southern flank as far as the eastern end, where flying buttresses rise above a small square generous with flowers, benches, and travelers taking their ease. The mood here often feels more peaceful than Notre-Dame's interior, where getting stuck behind a crush of tourists aiming cameras at the stained glass is almost inevitable.

name: Square Rene Viviani
short_description: Small Left Bank square adjacent to Saint-Julien-le-Pauvre, home to the oldest tree in Paris (a Robinia planted in 1601), with a bronze fountain depicting the legend of Saint-Julien.

beats.script_body: The Gothic glory of Notre-Dame de Paris presents a dramatic angle to this small Left Bank square along the Seine. Any weekday around noon, a few Parisians sit under the trees, reading, painting watercolors; children chase pigeons, a tourist eats a salad. There's a tall bronze fountain in the center — by Georges Jeanclos, 1995 — that tells the story of Saint-Julien le Pauvre, the name of the small church in the square's southwest corner, perhaps the oldest in the city. It was built in 1170–1240 on the ruins of the sixth-century church of Saint-Julien the Martyr.

beats.script_body:
Up close on the fountain you see sculpted images, motifs of the medieval legend about Saint-Julien: a stag, drops of tears, a river, a forest, as well as words from the adaptation by Gustave Flaubert, "The Legend of Saint Julien," in his Three Tales (1876). A traveler made curious by the fountain's inscription could pick up a copy of the Flaubert collection in the nearby bookstore Shakespeare and Company, a few minutes' walk to the west on rue de la Bucherie, and then follow Flaubert's retelling while studying the images and words on the fountain.

It's a religious story, unusual for Flaubert, appropriate to the place where the ancient church and the new fountain remember it: Julien, a "savage heart," possessed of a blood thirst similar to a wild animal's, murders his parents. He repents, lives alone in the wild, becoming a poor Hospitaller who devotes himself to helping lepers and ferrying them and other poor travelers across a river. At the end, there is a mystical and tender scene of transformation — a leper, who is Christ himself, embraces Julien and, in Flaubert's words, "the firmament unfolded — and Julian rose up into the blue of space, face to face with Our Lord Jesus, who bore him off to heaven."

The decorations on the fountain evoke a tradition of tendresse and compassion that Square René-Viviani commemorates. An annex of the Hôtel-Dieu, the public hospital for the poor, once stood here. And the square is named for the politician who, with Jean Jaurès and Nobel Peace Prize winner Aristide Briand, founded the Socialist Party of France, originally intended to provide a network of helping services for workers and for people who had nothing.

name: Shakespeare and Company
short_description: Legendary English-language bookshop on the Left Bank where writers can sleep among the stacks as 'tumbleweeds'

beats.script_body: A scruffy English-language bookshop packed from floor to ceiling with new and used books at 37, rue de la Bucherie. The descendant of the original shop in rue de l'Odéon where owner and publisher Sylvia Beach published James Joyce's Ulysses in 1922. A fun place on Bloomsday, June 16, with readings and wine-tasting upstairs. There's a good selection of books about Paris on the right wall as you enter.

corrections.corrected_text: The current Shakespeare and Company (37 rue de la Bûcherie) was opened by George Whitman in 1951 as 'Le Mistral' and renamed in Sylvia Beach's honor in 1964. Beach's original shop was at 12 rue de l'Odéon; it closed in 1941. The two shops are not under the same ownership — the current shop is a spiritual, not direct business, descendant.

queue_basis: A tiny bookshop that caps how many people fit inside and meters entry through one narrow door, so a short line forms at midday tourist peaks but clears quickly at opening; no security screening.

name: Memorial des Martyrs de la Deportation
short_description: Stark underground memorial at the tip of Ile de la Cite honouring the 200,000 people deported from France to Nazi concentration camps

beats.poi_name: Memorial des Martyrs de la Deportation
beats.script_body: Off Square de l'Île de France, at the eastern tip of Île de la Cité — cross Quai Archevêque and enter the small rose garden, surrounded by the Seine and facing Île Saint-Louis. Beneath the garden, down a narrow staircase, the writings on the walls of the memorial to the French martyrs of the Nazi Deportation are by Eluard, Saint-Exupéry, Sartre, Aragon, Desnos.

Narrow staircase descending to the underground memorial beneath the garden

beats.source_passage: LA MEMORIAL DES MARTYRS DE LA DEPORTATION Off Square de l'Ile de France, the eastern tip of lie de la Cite. Cross Quai Archeveque and enter the small rose garden (weekends, 8—9; weekdays, y:jo) surrounded by the Seine and facing lie Saint-Louis. Beneath the garden, down a narrow staircase, the writings on the walls of the memorial to the French martyrs of the Nazi Deportation are by Eluard, Saint-Exupery, Sartre, Aragon, Desnos.

opening_hours_basis: Door; hours are the place's own OpenStreetMap tag: Oct-Mar Tu-Su 10:00-17:00; Apr-Sep Tu-Su 10:00-19:00.
visit_basis: Stark underground memorial at the tip of Île de la Cité; you approach across the small garden above, then descend into the narrow crypt of 200,000 lights and inscriptions, a contemplative space taking about twenty minutes inside.
judgement_basis: This is a stark, silent underground memorial where running and casual conversation are socially unacceptable and there is no free open seating, and the site is closed and gated after dark.
queue_basis: The memorial is free but entered by a narrow staircase that admits only a few visitors at once, so a small line can form at midday while it is otherwise walk-straight-in.

name: Hotel-Dieu
short_description: Paris's oldest hospital, founded in the 12th century by Maurice de Sully.

beats.script_body: On the left of the plaza as you face the western front of Notre-Dame. Founded in 651 by Bishop Saint-Landry, Hôtel-Dieu (since rebuilt) is the oldest public hospital in Paris. Leave behind the hordes queuing for Notre-Dame, enter the lobby, and bear right, then left, into the lower garden. Go up the stairs to the larger upper garden, where you will find flowers and calm and a place to sit.

Founded in 651 by Bishop Saint-Landry, Hotel-Dieu (since rebuilt) is the oldest public hospital in Paris. Leave behind the hordes queuing for Notre-Dame, enter the lobby, and bear right, then left, into the lower garden. Go up the stairs to the larger upper garden, where you will find flowers and calm and a place to sit.

opening_hours_basis: An active hospital with a public inner courtyard/chapel behind entrances; gated, hours not confidently known; left unfiltered.
visit_basis: Working hospital with a long facade on the Notre-Dame parvis and an inner courtyard glimpse; it is not a visitor interior, so priced outside only.
judgement_basis: A functioning hospital with a quiet interior courtyard where running and casual sitting are inappropriate, but it sits on the open, lit, well-populated Ile de la Cite near Notre-Dame after dark.
queue_basis: A working hospital, not a ticketed attraction; a tourist stops to look at the facade and courtyard from the street and never joins any admission line.

name: Pont Neuf
short_description: Oldest surviving bridge in Paris built in 1578, the first stone bridge without houses on it, with 381 carved grotesque faces

beats.script_body: The large green standing boxes full of books and prints that line the quais on both banks of the Seine — les bouquinistes, the quintessentially Parisian version of bookselling — had their first location here on the Pont Neuf.

physical_cues.cue: The Seine quais visible from the bridge, lined with green book-stall boxes

inline_foreign_phrases.gloss: the quintessentially Parisian version of bookselling — open-air vendors with green box stalls on the quais

key_claims: Les bouquinistes — the large green standing boxes full of books and prints — line quais on both banks
The first bouquinistes were located on Pont Neuf
beats.source_passage: LES BOUQUINISTES The quintessentially Parisian version of bookselling. The large green standing boxes full of books and prints line the quais on both banks of the Seine. The first ones were located on Pont Neuf.

opening_hours_basis: Open street bridge crossable at any hour, not gated.
visit_basis: Oldest bridge in Paris with 381 carved grotesque faces and river views from its bays; a destination to walk across and pause on but nothing to enter.
judgement_basis: A stone road bridge with traffic down the middle and parapets straight onto the river where a running child is in danger, and its half-moon stone bays sit metres from moving cars making conversation an effort, but it is lit, open and centrally crossed at all hours.
queue_basis: A public bridge with no door and no ticket; the whole value stands in the open and there is no line.

anchors.label: Place Dauphine
anchors.basis: The triangular square opens off the bridge's mid-river terrace behind the Henri IV statue; a person steps off the bridge and stands inside the triangle to look at the brick-and-stone houses the corpus tells. Half the footprint reaches from the statue's steps into the square.

anchors.label: The Henri IV statue
anchors.basis: The bronze horseman stands on the terre-plein at the bridge's middle, directly above the steps down to the square du Vert-Galant — one standing position for both named spots, and a person looks at the statue from the platform around it.
